In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: R.
v. Bahr, 2006 ABPC 360

Date:

20061218

Docket:

050024363P101001

Registry:

Edmonton

Between:

Her Majesty The Queen

-
and -

Glenn David Bahr

Judgment of The
Honourable Judge M.G. Allen

Introduction

[
1
]

Glenn Bahr appeared before me at a preliminary inquiry charged with
wilfully promoting hatred contrary to
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
.
The alleged offence took place on a website.  In determining whether committal
is warranted a number of unique and complex issues require exploration.

[
2
]

Hereafter, reference to a section
number that is not attributed to any statute means a
Criminal Code

section.

An Overview of the
Evidence Related to Monitoring Websites

[
3
]

At the time of the offence, Sgt.
Stephan Camp was a hate crime investigator with the Edmonton Police Service.
He was monitoring a Website,
Stormfront
, which he believed to be a white
nationalist Website.
Stormfront
contained a Canadian forum where
individuals with access could post electronic messages.  These electronic
messages were accessible to any member of the public anywhere in the world,
through the use of the Internet.  In March 2004, Sgt. Camp saw an electronic
posting on
Stormfront
from an individual using the electronic moniker
SS-88 asking for, receiving, and acknowledging assistance related to the
creation of a new website,
Western Canada for Us
(
wcfu
).  On
March 8, 2004, Sgt. Camp noticed that SS-88 posted a message: “Our website is
on line.  Our website is now active.  I’m still adding content, et cetera.
Please come stop by and take part.  Thanks to Melissa from CHA for doing us
hosting and for the excellent tech support.  www.wcfu.com.  Wcfu, my honour is
my loyalty Heinrich Himmler SS Reich Fuhrer 88.”

[
4
]

Thereafter, Sgt. Camp monitored
the sections of the
wcfu
website available to the public; he visited
the website four days per week between March 8 and May 8, 2004.  The web page
(the opening document seen when a website is accessed) of
wcfu
contained
a number of links to other websites.  Sgt. Camp used those links to access
these latter websites.  On May 7, 2004, Sgt. Camp asked the technological
crime’s unit of the Edmonton Police Service to make a complete copy of the
sections of the website that were accessible to the public that day; Det. Shaji
Palamattam did so.  The accessible information captured was printed by the
Edmonton Police Service in a paper format.  Two binders of material, exhibits 8
and 9, were entered in evidence.

The Internet

[
5
]

A basic understanding of the
Internet is useful.  In the
Society of Composers, Authors and Music
Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Association of Internet Providers,
2004 SCC 45 (CanLII)
,
[2004]
2 S.C.R. 427 (S.C.C.)
(
SOCAN)

Binnie J., writing for the majority,
described the Internet in this way at paras. 8-9:

“The
Internet is a huge communications facility which consists of a worldwide
network of computer networks deployed to communicate information. A
“content provider” uploads his or her data, usually in the form of a website, to a host
server. The content is then forwarded to a destination computer (the end user).
End users and content providers can connect to the Internet with a modem under
contract with an Internet Service Provider.

An
Internet transmission is generally made in response to a request sent over the
Internet from the end user (referred to as a “pull”). The host server
provider transmits content (usually in accordance with its contractual
obligation to the content provider).” .
. .

[
6
]

Each website has a domain name or
address.  Generally one can communicate with a website by entering the domain
name address or key words into a search engine.  The first document seen upon
accessing most websites is a web page or home page.  Once a web page is
located, the user can click a computer mouse on the icons or blue underlined
words found on the web page.  Further information is then available for viewing
or retrieval.

wcfu
Web Page: Overview

[
7
]

In this instance, the police
investigators used
Google,
a commercial search engine, to locate the

wcfu
website.  The first document viewed by them was the web page or home
page.  The officers were not members of
wcfu
and the information they
viewed was accessible to any member of the public, in Canada or anywhere in the
world, who navigated the Internet to find the
wcfu
web page.  Det. Pal
Shaji Palamattam downloaded or electronically captured the information on the
Web page that was accessible to the public.  A hard copy of this information
was entered as exhibit 8 and 9 in the preliminary.

[
8
]

The middle of the home page contains
a welcoming statement:

“Western
Canada for Us fights for Freedom of Speech and Immigration Reform.  We also
believe
Euro-Canadians are fast
becoming a minority in Canada and we want to stop this decline and preserve our
heritage and history.  Because we are not a political party or religious group
WCFU can act as an umbrella group for other organizations.  We can also work
with other groups and organizations to provide support and unity.

United
we are a voice to be heard in Western Canada.

Our
goal is to unite the western provinces (British Columbia, Alberta,
Saskatchewan, and Manitoba) in an effort for Euro-Canadians to have a voice in
Western Canada.  We are an active group which means we hold protests,
demonstrations, distribute literature and hold monthly meetings.  Each Western
province is headed by a chapter providing local support and membership.  The
Alberta chapter is the head chapter of WCFU.  This is where the final decisions
are made.”

[
9
]

The main menu is on the right hand
side of the home page.  The main menu is subdivided into various sections:
Home, Image Gallery, Alberta Chapter, British Columbia Chapter, Forum,
Articles, Downloads, Links, FAQ’s (Frequently Asked Questions).

[
10
]

Sgt. Camp was questioned at length
on his grounds to support the charges.  He testified that he was concerned with
some of the material he found, within some of the following sections, and
believed that it might have constituted evidence supporting a charge pursuant
to
s. 319(2)
: Articles, Downloads, Links and the Forum.

[
11
]

While the officer’s opinion is
helpful in focusing on the possible offending statements, it is not, in any
manner, determinative as to whether this is evidence that supports a committal
for trial for the offence of wilful promotion of hatred, contrary to
s.
319(2)
.  Committal for trial is based an understanding of the test for
committal and the elements of the offence itself.

The Search Warrant

[
12
]

On May 7, 2004, Sgt. Camp applied for, and obtained, a search warrant to
enter the residence of the accused.

[
13
]

Sgt. Camp and other police
officers entered the premises pursuant to the search warrant.  The warrant
authorized the seizure of “computer equipment, including magnetic or other
machine readable storage equipment, digital cameras or other recording devices,
programs, or software associated with the said statement or any other device
and associated software and manuals used or capable of being used to create,
store, and manipulate electronic documents, records, files and other source
materials related to the persons and time frames in question.”  Pursuant to
that warrant, the computer towers were seized.

[
14
]

When Sgt. Camp and other officers
attended at that residence, they found Mr. Bahr at home.  Cst. Huggins seized a
number of items from the residence.  From a bedroom in the residence, Cst.
Huggins seized two computers towers from two different computers: a Seanix
model and a Dell computer.  He found mail addressed to the accused within that
same bedroom.

[
15
]

Det. Palamattam later examined the
computer towers, which contained the hard drives of each computer.  He made an
exact copy of the contents.  Det. Palamattam gave evidence as to those
contents.  He explained that each computer created a temporary Internet folder
which stored copies of any files that the user had visited.  Other temporary
Internet folder stored pages of electronic transmissions, sent from someone
using the electronic monikers SS-88skin@hotmail.com and glennbahr@yahoo.com.
Amongst those transmissions were transmissions sent to the
wcfu
website
as administrator, and as a participant in the Forum.  In addition, the folder
contained email messages sent to
Yahoo
, for the purpose of setting up
accounts, and messages transmitted between “Melissa” and Glenn Bahr.

Seizure of the Computer
Towers

[
16
]

Mr. Christie took issue with the
legality of the police search in relation to the police retrieving the contents
of the hard drive of these computers.  The evidence of Det. Palamattam, in this
regard, was not the subject of an objection when it was elicited by the Crown
in evidence in chief.  However, I take it that Mr. Christie believed that,
despite the admission of the evidence, I ought to properly disregard that
evidence in making my decision relating to committal.  His actual submission
will be set out under the next heading.  Set out below is summary of relevant
Criminal
Code

sections, and reference to the relevant jurisprudence.

[
17
]

Section 487(1)
governs the issuing of search warrants.

It
allows a justice or provincial court judge to issue a search warrant to police
officers to seize something in a building or place that will afford evidence,
on reasonable grounds, of the commission of an offence contrary to the
Code
.

Sections 487(2.1)
and
487(2.2)
deal with search warrants
authorizing searches of computer systems.
Subsection (2.1)
sets out the
scope of the actions that a person “authorized
under this section to search a computer system in a building or place for data” may take, whereas
subsection (2.2)
is
triggered when a warrant is presented to a "person who is in possession or
control or any building or place in respect of which a search is carried out
under this section.”  The provisions
vary to the extent that
ss. (2.1)
permits the reproduction, seizure and
copying of data in the form of a
print‑out or other intelligible
output
, whereas
ss. (2.2)
specifies that a
hard copy
of the
data to be obtained, seized, and copied.  At first glance,
ss. (2.1)
seems
to have wider scope in that the warrant authorizes a search for any data
contained
in the computer system
, or
available to it.  Subsection
(2.2)
contemplates a search of data contained in or available to the
computer system "that the person is authorized by this section to search
for" and at first glance, might thereby appear narrower in scope than s.
(2.1)
.
Yet the latter phrase appears to refer back to the warrant contemplated in s.
(2.1)
,
which authorizes the search of "a computer system in a building or
place."   These latter two subsections do not directly authorize the
police, while armed with a search warrant, to seize a computer; rather, the
provisions allow police who have a search warrant, which grants them the
authorization to search a computer system, with the ability to carry out the
search and exercise incidental  investigatory powers, at the scene of the
computer system.  It seems to me that Parliament would not have enumerated such
powers if they also intended that the police would be required to obtain an
authorization to intercept private communications, pursuant to
Part VI
,
in
the circumstances contemplated in ss. (2.1) and (2.2)
.

[
18
]

The police in this instance seized
the computer towers containing the hard drive, and made copies of the contents
while the towers were in police hands.  Although there is no specific
Code

provision allowing them to do so, the jurisprudence supports their ability to
do so.

[
19
]

In R.
v. Weir
(2001),
2001 ABCA 181 (CanLII)
,
156
C.C.C. (3d) 188 (Alta. C.A.)
the Court observed  at para. 19:

“The
police had a warrant to seize the computer from the appellant's home. That is
exactly what they did. As long as the CPU was seized properly, the information
contained in it could be extracted at a later date. To adopt the analogy used
by the trial judge, this is not unlike the seizure of blood in which police do
not want the blood, but rather, the information that the blood can provide.”

[
20
]

It is my view that here, the
seizure of the computer towers, and the steps taken by Det. Palamattam to
obtain the information, were allowed by the terms of the warrant.  However, a
further issue needs to be explored, i.e., if the folders contained private
communications that were intercepted by the police.  This issue will be
explored immediately below.

Counsel Submission Related
to Private Communication

[
21
]

Mr. Christie took the position
that the police had breached the
Code
, during their investigation,  by
intercepting private communications from Mr. Bahr’s computers.  Mr. Christie
conceded that the police had obtained the computer towers by a search warrant.
However, he pointed out that the search warrant did not specifically authorize
the police to decrypt or access private information.  He submitted that the
retrieval of the information by Det. Palamattam amounted to an interception of
private communications.  The
Code
prohibits the interception of a
private communication, absent authorization.  Thus, Mr. Christie submitted that
any information gained by the police in this way ought not to be admissible
here.

[
22
]

Certainly the issue raised is
interesting.  It requires me to consider the evidence and
Criminal Code

sections
related to the submission.

[
23
]

I first refer to the
Code

provisions referenced by Mr. Christie, and the other
Code
provisions.

Section 342.1

[
24
]

Mr. Christie referred to
s.
342.1(1)(b)
which applies to  “everyone, who, fraudulently and without
colour of right by means of an electromagnetic, acoustic, mechanical or other
device intercepts or causes to be intercepted, directly or indirectly any
function of a computer system.”  The terminology used in
s. 342.1(1)
is
defined within the
section
.  “Computer system” is defined, in part, “ as
a device that, or a group of interconnected or related devices one or more of
which contains computer programs or other data.”  “Electromagnetic, acoustic,
mechanical or other device” means “any device or apparatus that is used or is
capable of being used to intercept any function of a computer system. . . .”
“‘Intercept’ includes listen to or record a function of a computer system, or
acquire the substance, meaning or purport thereof.”

[
25
]

It would appear to me that
s.
342.1
is inapplicable.  The section is found in
Part IX
of the
Code

which deals with offences against property.  Most of the surrounding
sections deal with fraud or theft.  A closely aligned section,
s. 342,
creates
an offence where someone steals, forges, falsifies, possesses, uses or traffics
in a credit card.  Generally,
s. 342.1
would be used to prosecute
individuals who obtain a function or service with a view to economic
deprivation of the victim.  However, it is arguable that it could be used in
other circumstances.  The section contains the phrase “ fraudulently and
without colour of right.”  “Fraudulently” for the purpose of theft is “ an intentional
misappropriation without mistake”:
R. v. Skalbania
(1997),
1997 CanLII 337 (SCC)
,
120 C.C.C.
(3d) 217 (S.C.C.)
per McLachlin J. at p. 219.  Thus, the police
misappropriation of the information might be termed “fraudulent. “ The meaning
of “colour of right” was
considered in
R. v. DeMarco
(1973),
1973 CanLII 1542 (ON CA)
,
13 C.C.C.
(2d) 369 (Ont. C.A.)
.  Martin J.A. at p. 322 observed:

“The
term ‘colour of right’ generally, although not exclusively, refers to a
situation where there is an assertion of proprietary or possessory right to the
thing which is the subject matter of the alleged theft.  One who is honestly
asserting what he believes to an honest claim cannot be said to act ‘without
colour of right’ even though it may be unfounded in law or fact . . . The term
‘colour of right’ is also used to denote an honest belief in a state of facts
which, if was actually existed would in law justify or excuse the act done . .
. The term when used in the latter sense is merely a particular application of
the doctrine of mistake of fact.”

[
26
]

In my view, the evidence did not
establish that the police were acting without colour of right; rather, the
evidence established that Det. Palamattam honestly believed that he was
entitled to obtain the relevant information.

Are the Comments on the
Website “Private Communications”?

[
27
]

My finding that
s. 342.1
is
inapplicable does not end the matter.

[
28
]

Section 319(2)
does not apply to “private conversation.”  An ordinary
grammatical meaning of “conversation” would not normally bring anyone to
consider electronic transmissions a “private conversation.”
In
R. v.
Keegstra,

1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 697 (S.C.C.)
, which is the leading case related
to
s. 319(2),
Chief Justice Dickson, writing for the majority, held that
the term “private conversation” in
s. 319(2)
was akin to  “private
communication” as set out in
s. 183.
At p. 772-3 he wrote:

“The
provision [
s. 319(2)
]
does not prohibit views expressed with an
intention to promote hatred if made privately
, indicating Parliament’s
concern not to intrude upon the privacy of the individual.  Indeed, that the
legislation
excludes private conversation, rather than including communications made in a
public forum,
suggests that the expression of hatred in a place accessible
to the public is not sufficient to activate the legislation. . .  The
observation is supported by comparing the words of s. 319(2) with those of the
prohibition of public incitement of hatred likely to lead to a breach of the
peace in s. 319(1).  Section 319(1) covers the statements communicated “in any
public place”suggesting that a wider scope of prohibition was intended by the
danger occasioned by statements was of an immediate nature while the wording of
s. 319(2) indicates that private conversations taking place in public areas are
not prohibited.  Moreover, it is reasonable to infer a subjective mens rea
requirement regarding the type of conversation covered by s. 319(2), and
inference supported by the definition of “private conversation” contained
within
s. 183
of the
Criminal Code
.
Consequently, a conversation or
communication intended to be private does not satisfy the requirements of the
provision
if through accident or negligence an individual’s expression of
hatred is made public.”  [My underlining for emphasis].

[
29
]

Later,
in
R. v. Goldman,
(1979),

1979 CanLII 60 (SCC)
,
13 C.R. (3d) 228 (S.C.C.)
(
Goldman)
, McIntyre J., writing for the
majority, indicated that “private communications” and “private conversations”
had slightly different meanings.  A “communication” involved the passing of
thoughts, ideas, words or information from one person to another, whereas
“conversation” is a broader term and would include an interchange of a series
of communications: see p. 248.
Goldman
dealt with a distinction that
the Crown wished the court to make so as to exempt the authorities from the
need to obtain a wiretap order.  It does not contradict the comments of Dickson
C.J.
in
Keegstra
of the utility of the terminology in
Part VI
as
a contextual background to the meaning of the term “private conversation” in
s.
319(2)
.

[
30
]

In
R. v. Ahenakew,
[2006]
S.J. No. 354 (Sask. Q.B.)
(
Ahenakew
)
Laing C.J. dealt with an individual
who expressed allegedly hateful statements to a reporter during an interview.
At paras. 17- 18 he wrote:

“Counsel
for the appellant submitted that a conversation between any two persons, even
if one of them is a reporter, is a private conversation unless the person asks
the reporter to publish it. His point is that there are no members of the public
present during a two-person conversation, and what a reporter chooses to do
with the information received in the context of s. 319(2) is not the
responsibility of the speaker. In effect, counsel for the appellant advances
the same theme that arises in the third ground of appeal that the
actus reus

of the offence in s. 319(2) was committed by the reporter, Mr. Parker, and
not by the appellant because he is the person who published the appellant's
statements to the public. I am not able to accept this submission.

The
word ‘private’ in everyday usage means ‘not open to or intended for the
public,’ and this meaning is the generic meaning attributed to the word when
used as an adjective in most, if not all, dictionaries. This is clearly the
meaning of the word ‘private’ adopted by Dickson C.J. in the quote from
R v.
Keegstra
, supra
. It is also the meaning that a plain reading and a
purposive reading of s. 319(2) mandates. A private conversation is a
conversation not open to, or intended for, the public. The number of persons
present is irrelevant to the determination of whether a conversation is
private.”

[
31
]

Mr. Christie also relied upon the
provisions of
Part VI
to underline the illegality of the police action.

Section 184(1)
prohibits everyone from intercepting a private
conversation.  Pursuant to
s. 186
, a judge as defined in
s. 185

(in Alberta a Queen’s Bench Justice), may authorize an interception of private
communications in relation to certain offences named in
s. 183
.
The
list of offences does not include
s. 319(2)
.  In
s. 183
intercept
“includes listen to, record or acquire a communication or acquire the
substance, meaning, or purport thereof.”  “Private communication” is defined as
meaning, in part, “any telecommunication, that is made by an originator who is
in Canada . . . and that is made under circumstances in which it is reasonable
for the originator to expect it will not be intercepted by any person other
than the person intended by the originator to receive it.”

[
32
]

In

Goldman
McIntyre J.
explained that it is the originator’s state of mind under the definition of
“private communication” that is decisive: see p. 246.  In my view some of the
transmissions sent by Mr. Bahr to the
wcfu
were not intended by him to
be private.

[
33
]

In some instances Mr. Bahr sent
email to
wcfu
for inclusion on one of the threads on the Forum.  Any
member of the public who wished to do so could access the Forum section; by
making selections of a particular thread or theme they were able to view all
electronic posts on the thread.  Mr. Bahr made posts to a number of great
number of threads by email using the computers seized by the police.  Mr. Bahr
was the designer and administrator of the website.  The website was designed so
that the public could view posts on the Forum.  Indeed, anyone who sent emails
for inclusion would be aware of the public nature of the display of these on
the website.  In such circumstances, the telecommunication was not one where
the originator reasonably expected his emails only to be intercepted by the
recipient.  Rather, their expectation would that they would be on public
display or intercepted by others. I use
intercepted
in the inclusive
sense set out in
s. 183
as acquiring the meaning or substance of the
message.

Intercept

[
34
]

Mr. Bahr did send email messages
to “Melissa” and his own website by means of email.  Det. Palamattam did not
believe these communications to be private because he believed that only
encrypted email would not be capable of being intercepted.  While, technically,
that may be true, the email was a private communication because the evidence
reveals that the originator of those messages did not intend that they be
intercepted.

[
35
]

The issue to be determined in
relation to those messages is whether Det. Palamattam intercepted
communications, by using electronic means to locate them within the files or
folders on the accused’s computers.

[
36
]

A wider examination of the meaning
of the word “intercept” is necessary to determine this.  It must be remembered
that “intercept” is not defined in s. 183; rather, certain actions are included
within the meaning of the word.  Where a term is not defined in legislation,
the meaning of the term is found by examining the terms “in their entire
context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the
scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament”: see

Bell ExpressVu Limited Partnership v. Rex
,
[2002] 2 S.C.R. 559
,
2002 SCC
42
, at para.
26
, quoting E.A. Driedger,
Construction of Statutes
(2nd
ed. 1983), at p. 87; see also
Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd. (Re)
,
1998 CanLII 837 (SCC)
,
[1998]
1 S.C.R. 27
, at para.
21
.

[
37
]

In the text,
Wiretapping and
Electronic Surveillance Law and Procedure,
the authors refer to American
jurisprudence related to legislation dealing with the term “interception.”
Generally speaking, the United States jurisprudence rejected a view that the
term implies “contemporaneity”: pp. 15-18.5 - 15-18.6.  However, the authors also
pointed out that the American jurisprudence supported a view that a retrieval
by the police from files stored within a computer was not an interception.  The
point was discussed at p 15-13:

“.
. . The Court noted that there is a substantial difference between intercepting
electronic communications such as e‑mails and accessing electronic
communications in storage.  It held that a statutory interpretation of the
amended ECPA clearly demonstrates that Congress did not intend for the word
"intercept" to apply to electronic communications in storage.  The
court contrasted the substantive and the procedural requirements necessary for
authorizing
interception
of communications and those needed
for
accessing
stored electronic
communications. . . .”

[
38
]

The legislative scheme in Canada
is somewhat different from that of the United States.  The Supreme Court has
also recognized that, in
Part VI ,
Parliament meant to reconcile the
interest of the police in investigating crime with the right of privacy of the
individual, by providing that the police must always seek prior judicial
approval before employing using electronic surveillance: per La Forest J.
in
R.
v. Duarte
(1990),
1990 CanLII 150 (SCC)
,
53 C.C.C. (3d) 1 (S.C.C.)
at pp. 11-12
.

[
39
]

The Alberta Court of Appeal has
held that an interception must be contemporaneous with the electronic
transmission to amount to an interception:
R. v. McQueen,
1975 CanLII 1373 (AB SCAD)
,
[1975] 6
W.W.R. 604 (Alta. C.A.)
.  McDermid J.A., writing for the majority, explored the
ordinary meaning of the word by resorting to dictionary definitions.  He
concluded at p. 606:

“At
least in its primary sense, the word intercepts suggests that there must be an
interference between the place of origin and the place of destination of the
communication. “

[
40
]

Later, at p. 607 he added:

“The
legislation is aimed at preventing a third party intercepting the private
communication between two people.”

[
41
]

McQueen
was adopted as being correct by the British Columbia
Court of Appeal
in
R. v. Singh
(1998),
1998 CanLII 4819 (BC CA)
,
127 C.C.C.(3d) 429 (B.C.C.A.)
.

[
42
]

In this instance, the police
retrieved copies of the email messages sent and received by Mr. Bahr from files
or folders created by Mr. Bahr’s computer.  The ordinary grammatical meaning of
“intercept” suggests an interference between the place of origin and the place
of destination.
In
McQueen
the Court accepted that meaning.  This
meaning of the term means that the interference must be contemporaneous with
the transmission between the sender and receiver.  The police did not
interfere, in that manner, between the originator’s message and the sender’s
receipt of the message; rather, they retrieved copies of those messages from
files or folders created automatically by Mr. Bahr’s computers.  Even if the
American view that the interception need not be contemporaneous with the
transmission were to be the law, it is my view that the retrieval would not be
an interception.

[
43
]

This view of the law is consistent
with the intention of Parliament.  Parliament allows police officers armed with
a search warrant to search computers systems at the place where the search is
authorized, and requires those in control of the place searched to co-operate
in the retrieval of information:
s. 487(2.1)
and

“While

presumed not to intend to do so, in the absence of clear words or necessary

a connecting factor than the point of origin (not to mention the physical

1998 CanLII 818 (SCC)

Morguard
Investments

supra

Hunt v. T&N plc

1993 CanLII 43 (SCC)

supra

[2001] 3 S.C.R. 907,

[

Section 548(1)
(a)

Criminal Code

provides the standard that

provides, in part:

“When

(a)

the offence charged or any other indictable offence in respect of the same
transaction, order the accused to stand trial; or”

[
70
]

The meaning of the words have been
explored by the Supreme Court.  The seminal judgment related to the meaning of
the test is found in the majority decision of Ritchie J. in
The United
States of America v. Shephard
1976 CanLII 8 (SCC)
,
[1977] 2 S.C.R. 1067 (S.C.C.)
(
Shephard)
.
Ritchie J. explained the test and how it is to be applied.  The test is “
whether or not there is any evidence upon which a
reasonable jury properly instructed could return a verdict of guilty.”  The preliminary judge must commit for trial “in any case in which there is admissible evidence
which could, if it were believed, result in a conviction”: see p. 1080 of
Shephard
.

[
71
]

In
R. v. Arcuri,
2001 SCC 54 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 2
S.C.R. 828 (S.C.C.)
(
Arcuri
)
the Supreme Court unanimously confirmed the
test as set out by Ritchie J.  Chief Justice McLachlin wrote the decision of
the court.  At paras. 23 and 24 she explained that where there is
circumstantial evidence the test is still the same but the task of the judge is
somewhat more complicated:

“The
test is the same whether the evidence is direct or circumstantial:
see
Mezzo v. The Queen
,
1986 CanLII 16 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 802, at pp. 842-43;
Monteleone
,
supra
,
at p. 161. The nature of the judge’s
task, however, varies according to the type of evidence that the Crown has
advanced. Where the Crown’s case is
based entirely on direct evidence, the judge’s task is straightforward. By definition, the only conclusion that
needs to be reached in such a case is whether the evidence is true: see
Watt
’
s Manual of Criminal Evidence
(1998), at §8.0
(“[d]irect evidence is evidence which,
if believed, resolves a matter in issue”);

McCormick on Evidence
(5th ed. 1999), at p. 641; J. Sopinka, S. N.
Lederman and A. W. Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
(2nd ed. 1999),
at §2.74 (direct evidence is witness
testimony as to “the precise fact which
is the subject of the issue on trial”).
It is for the jury to say whether and how far the evidence is to be believed:
see
Shephard
,
supra
, at pp. 1086-87. Thus if the judge determines
that the Crown has presented direct evidence as to every element of the offence
charged, the judge’s task is complete.
If there is direct evidence as to every element of the offence, the accused
must be committed to trial.

The
judge’s task is somewhat more
complicated where the Crown has not presented direct evidence as to every
element of the offence. The question then becomes whether the remaining
elements of the offence – that is,
those elements as to which the Crown has not advanced direct evidence – may reasonably be inferred from the circumstantial
evidence. Answering this question inevitably requires the judge to engage in a
limited weighing of the evidence because, with circumstantial evidence, there
is, by definition, an inferential gap between the evidence and the matter to be
established – that is, an inferential
gap beyond the question of whether the evidence should be believed: see
Watt
’
s Manual of Criminal Evidence
,
supra
, at §9.01 (circumstantial evidence is “any
item of evidence, testimonial or real, other than the testimony of an
eyewitness to a material fact. It is any fact from the existence of which the
trier of fact may infer the existence of a fact in issue”);
McCormick on Evidence
,
supra
, at
pp. 641-42 (“[c]ircumstantial evidence
. . . may be testimonial, but even if the circumstances depicted are accepted
as true, additional reasoning is required to reach the desired conclusion”). The judge must therefore weigh the evidence, in
the sense of assessing whether it is reasonably capable of supporting the
inferences that the Crown asks the jury to draw. This weighing, however, is
limited. The judge does not ask whether she herself would conclude that the
accused is guilty. Nor does the judge draw factual inferences or assess
credibility. The judge asks only whether the evidence, if believed, could
reasonably support an inference of guilt.”

[
72
]

Later, at paras. 29-30, McLachlin
C.J. explained how exculpatory defence evidence is to be considered in
determining committal, and restated the limited weighing to be performed by the
preliminary inquiry judge:

“The
question that arises in the case at bar is whether the preliminary inquiry
judge
’s task differs where the defence
tenders exculpatory evidence, as is its prerogative under s. 541. In my view,
the task is essentially the same, in situations where the defence calls
exculpatory evidence, whether it be direct or circumstantial. Where the Crown
adduces direct evidence on all the elements of the offence, the case must
proceed to trial, regardless of the existence of defence evidence, as by
definition the only conclusion that needs to be reached is whether the evidence
is true. However, where the Crown’s
evidence consists of, or includes, circumstantial evidence, the judge must
engage in a limited weighing of the whole of the evidence (i.e.

including
any defence evidence) to determine whether a reasonable jury properly
instructed could return a verdict of guilty.

In
performing the task of limited weighing, the preliminary inquiry judge does not
draw inferences from facts. Nor does she assess credibility. Rather, the judge’s task is to determine whether, if the Crown’s evidence is believed, it would be reasonable for a
properly instructed jury to infer guilt. Thus, this task of “limited weighing” never requires consideration of the inherent reliability of the
evidence itself. It should be regarded, instead, as an assessment of the
reasonableness of the inferences to be drawn from the circumstantial evidence.”

was directly wilfully promoting hatred against identifiable groups.  In thread
48, he expressed the view that homosexuals should be killed; in thread 15 it
could be inferred that he was promoting death to Israelis.  Obviously, the
comments which others posted on the website can support an inference that they
intended to wilfully promote hatred against a number of identifiable groups.
While Mr. Bahr is not the person who posted all of the hate propaganda, he has
some responsibility for its presence.  He designed the website so that
individuals could post their views.  He was the main administrator of the

wcfu
website, and had the ability to delete individual entries from the
website.  The evidence supported a view that the administrator was informed of
all entries which had been posted on the website since the time of his last
visit.  In addition, Mr. Bahr listed himself as the first moderator on
virtually all of the threads where the offensive statements were found.  A jury
properly instructed might reasonably infer that he subjectively desired the
promotion of hatred because he shared the views of those posting, or that he
reasonably foresaw that consequence when he continued to allow the posts to
remain on the website.

Conclusion

[7]

The task of a judge at a
preliminary inquiry is more limited than that of the trier of fact.  A
preliminary inquiry judge is required to determine if the Crown has satisfied
the Court that the evidence is sufficient to put an accused on trial for the
offence charged, or another offence with respect to the same transaction.
Committal for trial will result when there is admissible evidence which could,
if believed, result in a conviction.  The preliminary inquiry judge must commit
for trial where there is admissible evidence on all elements of the offence
charged, or an offence arising from the same transaction.  The task is the same
whether the case is based on direct or circumstantial evidence.  However, where
circumstantial evidence is tendered, the preliminary judge must engage in a
limited weighing of the circumstantial evidence to determine whether that
evidence is capable of supporting any inference that the Crown wishes the
preliminary judge to draw.  The limited weighing never requires the preliminary
inquiry judge to consider the inherent reliability of the evidence (this is a
task for the trier of fact); rather the limited weighing is an assessment of
the reasonableness of the inferences to be drawn from circumstantial evidence.

[8]

The Crown’s ability to prove these
elements is made more difficult because the alleged offence was committed
largely on a website which was probably located in another country.  A number
of somewhat unique issues needed exploration.

[9]

I have carefully considered the
facts in this case, the sections of the
Code
, and the relevant
jurisprudence.  For the reasons set out herein, I conclude that the evidence is
sufficient to commit for trial.  Therefore, Mr. Bahr is committed to stand
trial on the offence charged.
